claims.text: A multi-phase eutectic HEA can develop local galvanic coupling between phases because the phases have different electrochemical potentials.
Mechanical sliding repeatedly ruptures a protective surface oxide film.
Galvanic coupling and repeated oxide rupture accelerate metal dissolution and mechanical removal beyond the sum of separate wear and corrosion losses.
The relevant initial microstructure contains electrochemically dissimilar phases such as an FCC matrix and an intermetallic sigma phase.
The specimens should begin in an as-cast or as-clad condition without prior tribocorrosion damage.
The proposed intervention is simultaneous sliding and corrosive exposure at elevated temperature while controlling load, sliding speed, electrolyte composition, and temperature.
Chloride-containing media can provide conditions associated with galvanic corrosion in an FCC-plus-sigma eutectic HEA coating.
HEA coatings can exhibit substantial wear resistance at elevated temperature.
Galvanic activity and oxide-film disruption are concentrated along eutectic phase boundaries.
Mechanical rubbing induces microcracks in addition to rupturing the oxide layer.
Exposure of fresh metal after oxide rupture permits renewed oxidation and dissolution.
One phase selectively dissolves as a result of galvanic interactions between the FCC and sigma phases.
Corrosion-induced weakening increases subsequent mechanical wear under load.
Combined tribocorrosion produces statistically greater total material loss than the sum of matched wear-only and corrosion-only losses.
Under combined exposure, both the wear rate and corrosion rate increase relative to their respective independent values.
Combined exposure causes severe localized attack at phase boundaries.
The synergy should diminish when electrochemical contrast between phases is small or the environment is minimally corrosive.
Tribofilm formation and local temperature spikes may change the magnitude or direction of the coupled response.
A controlled comparison should include corrosion-only, wear-only, and simultaneous tribocorrosion tests on statistically identical specimens.
The synergistic hypothesis is falsified if combined degradation is not statistically greater than the summed separate losses within experimental error.

contradictions.description: The conditions define wear-only testing as having no solution, while the baseline says isolated tests retain the same environmental parameters, including solution. A wear-only test cannot simultaneously have no solution and the same solution exposure as the combined test.
